nameStory: Northern krill gets its straightforward name from being the dominant krill species in northern waters like the North Atlantic. The word 'krill' comes from the Norwegian word meaning 'small fry of fish,' which Norwegian whalers used to describe the tiny shrimp-like creatures that fed the great whales.
description: Northern krill are tiny, translucent shrimp-like creatures that drift through New England's coastal waters as part of the zooplankton. These small crustaceans have segmented bodies, multiple swimming legs, and large black eyes that give them an almost alien appearance. Though individually small, they often gather in massive swarms that can turn patches of ocean water orange or pink. They're essentially the 'potato chips' of the ocean - almost everything bigger than them wants to eat them!

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: Body is nearly see-through with a glassy, jellyfish-like transparency that lets you glimpse their internal organs as dark shadows

idTips.label: Large black eyes
idTips.description: Prominent compound eyes that appear as shiny black dots, almost comically large for their tiny body size

idTips.label: Swimming legs
idTips.description: Multiple pairs of feathery swimming legs (pleopods) that create a gentle rippling motion as they paddle through the water

idTips.label: Segmented body
idTips.description: Body divided into distinct segments like a tiny lobster, with a clearly separate head, thorax, and abdomen

idTips.label: Swarming behavior
idTips.description: Often found in dense clouds or patches that can color the water reddish-orange and feel slightly gritty if you run your hand through them

habitat: Northern krill live in the open waters off New England's coast, particularly in the cooler waters of the Gulf of Maine and outer continental shelf. They prefer the middle depths during the day but rise toward the surface at night, so you're most likely to spot them from boats in offshore waters rather than from shore.

seasonality.spring: Krill populations begin building as waters warm and phytoplankton blooms provide abundant food. Look for them in cooler offshore waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance when they're most visible in surface waters, especially during evening hours when they migrate upward to feed.
seasonality.fall: Still active and abundant as they continue feeding before winter. Often concentrated in areas where cold and warm water masses meet.
seasonality.winter: Present but typically in deeper waters and less visible from the surface due to their deeper distribution in cold months.

funFact: Northern krill can tolerate a remarkable temperature range from just above freezing to 59°F (15°C) - that's like being equally comfortable in an ice bath and a heated swimming pool, making them incredibly adaptable compared to their Antarctic cousins who would die in 'warm' 40°F water!
confusionNotes: Northern krill are most easily confused with other small zooplankton like copepods, but krill have the distinctive shrimp-like body shape with clear segmentation, while copepods are more teardrop-shaped. Remember: if it looks like a tiny translucent shrimp, it's probably krill; if it's more blob-like, it's likely a copepod.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being tiny individually, northern krill are absolutely crucial to New England's marine ecosystem - they're what connects the microscopic plant life in the ocean to everything we actually notice, from the fish we catch to the whales we watch. Without krill, the entire ocean food web would collapse.
compareHints: Northern krill is the only species in its genus Meganyctiphanes, making it unique in New England waters. Compared to other krill species in the euphausiid family, northern krill stands out for its exceptional temperature tolerance and ability to thrive in the variable conditions of the North Atlantic, whereas most krill species are adapted to much narrower temperature ranges.
